extracted.intended_audience: banks, credit unions, ABA members, and Federal Reserve/policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: A stakeholder (ABA) comment letter opposing the Federal Reserve's Regulation II proposal to lower Durbin debit interchange caps, arguing the proposal would harm the economics of low‑fee deposit products (especially Bank On accounts) and financial inclusion. The page provides the policy arguments and data points used to persuade regulators and industry members to oppose the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider consumer stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ensure that the Federal Reserve understands that consumers are stakeholders worthy of consideration."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Fed should explicitly weigh consumer interests when evaluating fee caps and not prioritize merchant/retailer interests alone. Policy analysis should include consumer welfare impacts (access, affordability, service availability) alongside merchant cost concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid large decreases in debit interchange caps
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal would impose "an almost 30% decrease in the debit interchange fee that covered banks and credit unions may receive for each debit transaction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators should not adopt reductions of this magnitude because such cuts threaten the economic viability of debit card products that support low‑fee accounts. Impact analyses should quantify how proposed percentage reductions affect issuer revenues and product viability across institution sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve public comment in routine reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal introduces "an automatic biennial review of these fee caps without accompanying public comment each time the caps are reviewed by the Federal Reserve."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any recurring review mechanism (e.g., biennial reviews) should include opportunities for public notice and comment. The Fed should retain procedural safeguards to ensure stakeholders can submit evidence and respond to proposed changes during each review cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect the economic sustainability of Bank On‑certified accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Bank On accounts "have very low monthly and almost no ancillary fees" and "are largely supported through debit card activity"; the rule "will fundamentally impair the sustainability of affordable deposit account products."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy decisions should ensure that revenue streams (notably debit interchange) that subsidize low‑fee/no‑fee accounts are preserved or replaced, so financial institutions can continue offering Bank On‑style accounts. Evaluations should consider whether a rule will make it infeasible for institutions to offer such accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess impacts on financial inclusion and unbanked households
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment cites that "In 2021, the unbanked rate fell to 4.5% – a record low – and 5 million unbanked households were newly banked" as evidence of progress that may be at risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators should analyze how proposed changes would affect unbanked and underbanked populations, including potential reversals of progress in account access. Quantitative metrics (unbanked rate, newly banked households, access to low‑cost accounts) should be part of the rulemaking record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid subsidizing large retailers at customers' expense
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal "will subsidize the largest global retailers at the expense of bank account customers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking should avoid tilting the balance of costs/benefits so that merchants capture savings while bank customers lose services or face degraded account offerings. Analyses should identify which parties bear costs and which reap benefits under proposed changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider effects across institutions of all sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: The rulemaking "jeopardizes consumers' ability to access safe and affordable banking products" and could undermine "financial institutions of all sizes to offer Bank On‑certified accounts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Fed should evaluate heterogeneous impacts on community banks, regional banks, and credit unions—not just large banks or merchants—and include institution‑level impact assessments to determine whether smaller institutions can sustain low‑fee products under the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid regulatory overreach that weakens product economics
rubrics_metrics.description: The letter warns of "regulatory overreach" that would "jeopardize the economic sustainability of Bank On accounts just as we are reaching nationwide availability."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators should be cautious about broad, aggressive interventions that disrupt existing business models which enable affordable banking products. Cost‑benefit and unintended consequences analyses should be robust and specifically address product sustainability and market availability.
